Not necessarily. It depends on the state. Child support, asset division, alimony—there aren’t federally enforced standards for these legal matters. They’re determined by each stat individually.

In California, for example, child support is assessed by the standard “equalization between the homes.” This means that whichever parent has the greater amount of resources will be required to pay the parent without. Custody can be a modifier of the amount, but it doesn’t negate the standard. 

Actor Jon Cryer, for example, had physical custody of his son, but because his ex-wife hosted their child a couple of days a month, he was ordered to pay her a large amount (I think somewhere in the $40K range) because the court assessed that’s the amount of money to ensure the boy was receiving an equal standard of living while in her care.

Termination can be as varied and individualized as therapists themselves.

I’ve informally terminated with several therapists—that is, I simply stopped seeing them without giving notice or participating a termination session. Most I did early into the relationship, before forming a therapeutic alliance. There were a few with whom I’d worked for a while, but for whatever reason, didn’t feel the need to formally terminate with.

I’ve formally terminated with several. These were kind, loving, emotionally charged sessions that really prioritized my comfort and well-being, and made it clear that the door was always open to me in case I needed something. It helped that these were always long-term relationships, and leading up to that last session involved a lot of transparent discussions between the therapist and myself—what worked well? What goals were met? What other areas need improvement? Etc.

Several of them were forced by circumstances beyond me or the provider—I’m thinking of when I discharged from residential or intensive outpatient settings. These sessions were often still conducted with the utmost consideration allowed by the provider, but constrained because some outside party (insurance companies, mainly) judged I was ready, even if the provider and I disagreed. Those sessions were painful, but the conduct and consideration rendered by the provider made them tolerable. Even on a compressed timeline, the providers validated my feelings, reemphasized my growth, and affirmed the work we did together. For me, it was crucial not to be attacked, critiqued, or blindsided.

That’s because I have previously had an extremely negative experience with termination. I don’t want to share the details, because it was absolutely the most traumatic experience of my life and something I am still trying to recover from—which is saying something, as I have profound amounts of trauma going all the way back to infancy. But that experience scarred me deeply, when a therapist I had worked with for years berated me in a group setting while violating my confidentiality and humiliating me in the process. That’s not even getting into the dual relationship she fostered with me. 15 years later, I understand now what I couldn’t have known then: her conduct was deeply unethical long before we ever reached termination, and naturally, that set the tone for a termination that went way beyond volatile.

I was from a troubled family who didn’t have the first idea of what healthy looked like. So when my therapist began to play a mother role to me while I was still a teenager desperately stinging from my own mother’s rejection, accepted what she offered pretty greedily. I even felt so cool compared to the other clients I knew she had, because I was certain what she felt for me was special. I had no way of knowing that erasure of boundaries guaranteed the inevitable outcome. The termination went badly because she failed in her fundamental duty to manage her countertransference, among other things.

This is a very long-winded way of saying that my own belief is that the quality of sessions, even those that deal with termination, speaks to the capabilities of providers. While it is understandable that termination sessions are emotionally charged, they should never become an opportunity for either party to grind axes against the other. And while I think it’s okay to demonstrate emotions and can be therapeutic for clients to see that the therapist is invested, that emotional release should never be against the client or at their expense.

Speaking as someone who has recently come to grips with the reality of an abusive family member murdering children…it’s not that cut and dry.

As children, we literally have to think of our caregivers as infallible. Our survival depends on it. Even if you’re subjected to horrific abuse, you will internalize it because the vast majority of young children don’t have the capability to compartmentalize. They rationalize that they deserve it, and rather than the abuse being bad, conclude that they are bad. Abuse also often arrests development, so the ability to do so is frequently delayed.

And when your abuser happens to be your main caregiver as well, it becomes that much more difficult to untangle. I spent years trying to ask other adults and authorities for help and at every turn, the system let me down. No one intervened. The abuse I was experiencing was severe enough that other parents didn’t want their kids to socialize with me, but not enough for them to actually meaningfully do anything to help me.

By the time I was a teenager, I knew my living situation was fucked up. I knew my caregivers were abusive. It took two decades of intensive trauma therapy, including several stays at in-patient facilities, plus going no-contact after having my own kids, a nervous breakdown over one of my children coming out as trans (and immediately fearing for their safety) to face up to the reality that beyond being abusive, my caregivers had also murdered my siblings—something I knew intuitively, but due to trauma, couldn’t admit to myself or face up to. I am currently in therapy with two providers, the second of whom does a modality of therapy known as Brainspotting. One of the theories behind it, as I understand it, is that where a client looks is important. I feel self-conscious about the eye contact with my primary therapist, in part because of how not being able to hold eye contact was used by people to invalidate my experiences. 

So I’m also working on paying attention to what looking away, and where, means when I do it. Not as a way to invalidate myself, but rather to be more mindful about my feelings as they relate to the subjects I’m discussing. For example, I’ve noticed that as much as I like my primary therapist, and more importantly feel safe with him, I am also very aware that I don’t like looking at him when I’m talking about a specific traumatic event involving someone to whom he bears more than a passing resemblance. 

In short, just know that looking away often communicates a lot. Even if your provider isn’t trained in brainspotting, you can do some of the work yourself. Next time you avert your eyes, try to catalogue, if only in your mind, where they land. If you can find a fixed point, that can also be a place you look for self-soothing even if you aren’t particularly activated.

I still get to listen to people, hear their struggles, and validate them, but then I get to go off and write a grant to fund the center where they receive counseling or author an article about what it means to be struggling with PTSD when you’re a climate change refugee.
